title: Mapping Non‐Human Primate Conservation Evidence in Tanzania's Eastern Arcs—Southern Highlands Ecosystem: A Systematic Review of Threats, Research Gaps and Recommended Strategies
content:
ABSTRACT

The Eastern Arcs—Southern Highlands (EASH) ecosystem of Tanzania constitutes a critical portion of the Eastern Afromontane Biodiversity Hotspot and supports several endemic and threatened primate taxa. While the region's exceptional non-human primate diversity is recognized, the absence of a regional synthesis of research efforts, documented threats, and conservation responses limits the identification of evidence gaps and the alignment of conservation actions with available ecological knowledge. We conducted a systematic review and evidence map of peer-reviewed and accessible grey literature to assess the state of knowledge on EASH primates. Following PRISMA guidelines, we screened 304 records, with 36 meeting our eligibility criteria. Our analysis revealed a fragmented and taxonomically biased knowledge base. Of the 90 species-occurrence records extracted, research attention was concentrated in Cercopithecidae (61.1%) and Colobidae (33.3%), whereas Galagidae accounted for only 5.6% despite comprising four documented species. Research effort was particularly concentrated on a few well-studied taxa, including Procolobus gordonorum (18 studies) and Rungwecebus kipunji (11 studies), while several nocturnal taxa were represented by minimal primary field research. The literature consistently identified interconnected hunting and habitat loss as dominant threats, while conservation recommendations focused primarily on legal protection and monitoring, with limited attention to specific threat mitigation or community-based approaches. This synthesis demonstrates that uneven evidence coverage may constrain conservation planning by leaving poorly studied taxa and locations underrepresented in decision-making. Addressing these gaps requires targeted ecological research on neglected taxa and integrated conservation strategies tailored to the socio-ecological complexities of the EASH region.
